title: Number of Digit One
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every digit of every number versus counting occurrences of 1 at each digit position directly.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Problem Summary: Given n, count the total number of times the digit 1 appears across every number from 1 up to n.

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Detail"],"rows":[["Pattern","Counting by digit position across an entire range at once, instead of checking every number individually; a place value formula with three cases based on the current digit."],["Difficulty","Advanced"],["Tags","Math"],["Interview Focus","Switching from \"number by number\" to \"digit position by digit position\" thinking, and correctly deriving and applying the three-case formula, current digit less than, equal to, or greater than 1."]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given a number n, count the total number of times the digit 1 appears across every number from 1 up to n. This is not counting how many numbers contain a 1, a number like 11 contributes two to the total, one for each 1 it contains.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting a Letter in a Giant Book
blocks.text: Picture a book that lists every number from 1 to n, one after another, and the task is to count every single appearance of the digit 1 anywhere in that entire book, the same way you might count how many times the letter "e" appears across every page. It does not matter which number a 1 belongs to, or how many 1s appear in the same number, every single occurrence adds one to the total.

blocks.caption: Count how many 1s appear at each digit position, then add them all up

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: n = 13
Adding up 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 (every other number from 1 to 13 contributes zero) gives a total of 6.
Example: n = 0
There are no positive numbers to check at all, so the answer is 0.
Example: n = 1
Only the number 1 exists in range, contributing exactly one 1, so the answer is 1.
5. How Should We Think?
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what "counting every 1" is really asking for.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Counting how many times the digit 1 appears requires looking at every digit of every number, but that does not mean the only way to do it is number by number.

Observation 2: Instead, the same total can be reached by fixing one digit position at a time, the ones place, the tens place, the hundreds place, and asking how many times, across the entire range from 1 to n, a 1 lands specifically in this position.

Observation 3: For a fixed position, every number can be split into three parts around it: the digits to the left (how many full higher groups exist), the single digit currently sitting at that position, and the digits to the right (how far into the current group we are).

Observation 4: Whether that position's digit is less than, equal to, or greater than 1 changes exactly how many of those higher groups get a full contribution versus a partial one, and that relationship can be captured in one small formula per position, computed directly with no scanning required.
That reasoning alone already replaces "check every number" with "compute each position's contribution directly."
6. Brute Force Solution
The most direct approach is to walk through every number from 1 to n, examine each of its digits individually, and add 1 to a running total every time a digit equals 1.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every number from 1 to n.
Look at each digit of that number one at a time, using modulo 10 and integer division by 10.
Every time a digit equals 1, add 1 to the running total.
Return the total once every number has been checked.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: examine every digit of every number individually

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The outer loop walks every number from 1 to n individually, since this version's whole strategy is to inspect each number's digits one number at a time, with no shortcuts.

The inner while loop peels digits off temp using modulo 10 and integer division by 10, a standard way to visit a number's digits from least significant to most significant without needing to know in advance how many digits it has.

A separate temp variable is used inside the inner loop specifically so number itself stays unchanged for the outer loop's own bookkeeping, since temp gets consumed, divided down to 0, during digit extraction.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
This works because it directly inspects every digit of every number in range, guaranteeing every occurrence of 1 is counted exactly once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), since there are n numbers, and each has roughly log n digits to examine.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: for large n, like a billion, examining every single number individually is far too slow. Instead of thinking number by number, it is possible to think digit position by digit position: for the units place, the tens place, the hundreds place, and so on, count directly how many times a 1 appears at that position across the entire range at once.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every number's every digit works but is slow: for a large n, like a billion, this means examining roughly a billion numbers, each with several digits, an enormous amount of individual work.

What is being recomputed unnecessarily: the same digit position, say the tens place, is revisited over and over, once per number, when its behavior across the whole range actually follows a predictable pattern.

Can a single digit position's contribution across the entire range be computed directly: yes, by splitting n around that position into the digits to its left, the digit at that position itself, and the digits to its right.

What determines the exact count at that position: whether the digit currently sitting there is 0, exactly 1, or greater than 1, each case having its own small formula.

The core idea: for each digit position from the ones place upward, compute that position's exact contribution directly with a formula, and sum across all positions.

For a fixed digit position with place value "base" (1 for units, 10 for tens, 100 for hundreds, and so on), n can be split into three parts around that position: the digits to the left (high), the single digit currently at that position (current), and the digits to the right (low). A clean formula, based on whether current is less than, equal to, or greater than 1, gives the exact count of 1s at that position across the whole range, in constant time per position.
9. Optimized Solution

For each place value, from the ones digit upward, split n into high, current, and low around that position. If current is 0, the count is high times base. If current is 1, the count is high times base, plus low, plus 1. Otherwise, the count is (high plus 1) times base. Sum this across every digit position.
Dry run for n = 13

blocks.content: {"headers":["base","high","current","low","Count at this position","Why"],"rows":[["1","1","3","0","(1 + 1) times 1 = 2","current is 3, greater than 1, so the final partial group at this position already counts as a full one."],["10","0","1","3","0 times 10 + 3 + 1 = 4","current is exactly 1, so the count includes the full groups plus every value the lower digits, low, can still take."]]}

blocks.text: Adding 2 + 4 gives 6, matching the brute force count exactly. The loop stops here since the next place value, 100, already exceeds n, so no further position contributes anything.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: count 1s at each digit position with a direct formula

blocks.text: Why This Works

This works because for a fixed place value, the numbers from 1 to n form repeating groups of size base times 10, and within each complete group, the digit at this position cycles through 0 through 9 exactly base times each; high counts how many complete groups exist, contributing high times base occurrences of the digit 1 at this position unconditionally. The final, partial group needs its own careful count based on what the current digit at that position actually is: if it equals 1, the partial group contributes every value of the lower digits, low plus 1, since those lower positions can range from all zeros up to the actual low value while this position sits at exactly 1; if it is greater than 1, the partial group has already fully passed through this position being 1, contributing one whole additional base worth of occurrences.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case (current digit at this position)","What It Means","Contribution"],"rows":[["Exactly 0","This position never reaches 1 in the final, incomplete group","high times base, only from complete groups"],["Exactly 1","The final, incomplete group does reach exactly 1 at this position, for every value of the lower digits up to low","high times base, plus low plus 1"],["Greater than 1","The final, incomplete group has already passed through this position being 1 entirely","(high plus 1) times base, treating the incomplete group as a full one for this position"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: base starts at 1 and is multiplied by 10 every iteration, walking through the ones place, tens place, hundreds place, and so on, exactly the sequence of positions that need to be summed over.
high, current, and low are all derived purely with integer division and modulo against base and base times 10, no digit array or string conversion needed at any point.
The loop condition base <= n is what naturally stops the process once every digit position that could possibly contain a nonzero digit of n has already been processed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n), a genuine complexity class improvement, since only one pass per digit position of n is needed, instead of one pass per number.
Space: O(1). This already matches the theoretical floor, since at least each digit position of n must be examined once.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

The core pattern here is switching from thinking number by number to thinking digit position by digit position, counting how a digit behaves across an entire range at once instead of checking every individual number. This same digit-position reasoning is a common building block in other "count digits across a range" style problems.
Common Mistakes

items: Mixing up the three formula cases (current less than 1, equal to 1, or greater than 1), which are each slightly different and easy to swap by accident.
Forgetting that the "current equals 1" case needs the extra plus 1 plus low term, unlike the other two cases.
Using int instead of a wider type for intermediate products, which can overflow for large n depending on the language.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["n = 0","Returns 0 immediately, since there are no positive numbers to check at all."],["n exactly at a power of 10, like 100","A good boundary case for the formula, since the current digit at several positions lands exactly on 0 or 1 in revealing ways."],["Large n","The gap between the brute force and the digit position approach becomes dramatic here, since one scales with n log n and the other with just log n."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips

This problem is one of the clearest examples of "counting by position instead of by item", a technique worth having ready whenever a problem asks for a count across a large range of numbers. Being able to derive the three formula cases from first principles, rather than reciting them from memory, is what separates genuine understanding from a memorized trick.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every number", think: count occurrences of 1 at each digit position directly, across the whole range at once.
If the interviewer says "can you derive the formula, not just state it", think: split n around each position into high, current, and low, and reason about how many complete versus partial groups reach a 1 there.
If the interviewer says "why three cases", think: whether the current digit is 0, exactly 1, or greater than 1 changes whether the final partial group reaches, exceeds, or never reaches a 1 at that position.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Can you derive the three-case formula from scratch, explaining why each case looks the way it does?
How would this approach generalize to counting occurrences of a digit other than 1?
Can you count occurrences of 1 within a specific range, from some L to some R, rather than always starting from 1?
What is the relationship between this problem's digit position technique and digit DP, dynamic programming over digit positions, used in harder counting problems?
How would you verify this formula's correctness for a range of small n values without trusting it blindly?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Digit DP, dynamic programming over digit positions, a more general technique for counting numbers satisfying digit based constraints across a range, of which this problem's direct formula is a simpler special case.
Any "count occurrences of X across a range of numbers" problem, which often becomes tractable by switching from per-number counting to per-position counting.
Counting multiples or specific patterns within a numeric range, which frequently reuses the same high, current, low decomposition around a fixed place value.
Number theory problems in general, where splitting a number by place value, rather than treating it as an opaque integer, unlocks a direct, closed form count.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force approach runs in O(n log n) time and O(1) space, examining every digit of every number individually. The digit position formula reaches O(log n) time and O(1) space, a genuine complexity class improvement, by counting occurrences of 1 at each place value directly instead of number by number.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: counting by digit position across an entire range at once, instead of checking every number individually.

Core Idea: for each place value, split n into the digits to the left, high, the digit at that position, current, and the digits to the right, low, then use a three-case formula, based on whether current is less than, equal to, or greater than 1, to count that position's contribution directly.
Time: O(n log n) for the brute force, O(log n) for the digit position formula.
Space: O(1) for both.

Most Important Observation: switching from number-by-number to position-by-position thinking turns a problem that looks like it needs n individual checks into one that only needs log n direct computations.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the brute force; deriving and correctly applying the three-case position formula is what demonstrates real command of digit based counting.
One line memory trick: for each place value, split into high, current, low, apply the three-case formula, and sum across all positions.
